summary.text: The ozone layer is a region of Earth's stratosphere, mostly about 15 to 35 km up, that absorbs most of the Sun's ultraviolet radiation.
It takes in 97 to 99 percent of the Sun's medium-frequency ultraviolet light, which would otherwise potentially damage exposed life near the surface.
In 1985 research showed industrial chemicals, mainly CFCs, were depleting it, which led to bans, and depletion now appears to have slowed or stopped.

paragraphs.heading: A shield of ozone
paragraphs.text: The ozone layer, also called the ozone shield, is a region of the stratosphere that takes in most of the ultraviolet (UV) radiation coming from the Sun. It holds more ozone (O₃) than other parts of the atmosphere, though ozone is still scarce next to the other gases around it. At its peak it reaches 8 to 15 parts per million of ozone, against about 0.3 parts per million for the atmosphere as a whole. Most of it lies in the lower stratosphere, roughly 15 to 35 km up, and its thickness changes with the seasons and from place to place.

paragraphs.heading: Found by missing light
paragraphs.text: The French physicists Charles Fabry and Henri Buisson discovered the layer in 1913. Measurements of sunlight reaching the ground matched the spectrum of a black body at 5,500–6,000 K, with one gap: no radiation arrived below a wavelength of about 310 nm, at the UV end. Scientists reasoned that something in the atmosphere was absorbing the missing light. Its pattern was finally matched to just one known chemical, ozone.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring it
paragraphs.text: The British meteorologist Dobson studied the layer's properties in detail. He built a simple spectrophotometer, the Dobsonmeter, which could measure ozone in the stratosphere from the ground. Between 1928 and 1958 he set up a worldwide network of ozone monitoring stations, and they still operate today. The Dobson unit (DU), a handy measure of how much ozone lies overhead, is named after him.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: It takes in 97 to 99 percent of the medium-frequency UV light from the Sun, from about 200 to 315 nm, which could otherwise harm exposed life near the surface. In 1985, research showed that chemicals released by industry, mainly chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), were depleting it. Fears that extra UV would threaten life, including more skin cancer in people, led to bans on these chemicals. The latest evidence is that the depletion has slowed or stopped, and each September 16 the United Nations holds its International Day for the Preservation of the Ozone Layer.
